query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the content of a selected dopant element (up to ~10 at.%) in a high-entropy-alloy (HEA) coating amplifies lattice distortion and stabilizes tribo-layers, leading to measurably improved wear performance under sliding conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited high-entropy-alloy coating (e.g., synthesized by sputtering from a baseline equiatomic HEA target) with minimal dopant content.
generation.intervention: Incrementally increase the dopant concentration (0–10 at.%) of a suitable element that enhances lattice strain while retaining single-phase stability.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature pin-on-disk or ball-on-disk wear tests under typical industrial loads (e.g., 1–5 N) and sliding speeds (e.g., 0.1–0.5 m/s), with systematic microstructural and tribochemical analyses (SEM, EDS, XRD) after testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion and subsequent formation/preservation of a more robust tribofilm at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: Dopant-induced lattice strain reduces the mobility of dislocations and promotes stable surface tribo-layer formation, thus mitigating material removal and lowering the steady-state friction coefficient.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, doped coatings exhibit lower wear rates and friction coefficients, combined with evidence of more resilient tribofilms in microstructural post-test analyses.
generation.baseline: Undoped or minimally doped HEA coatings of otherwise similar composition and synthesis conditions, exhibiting higher wear rates and less stable tribofilms.
generation.boundary: Effects are anticipated to hold for dopant concentrations up to ~10 at.% and under room-temperature or slightly elevated-temperature sliding conditions, as long as the single-phase HEA structure is preserved.
generation.uncertainty: Above ~10 at.% doping, excessive phase segregation may degrade mechanical properties and disrupt tribofilm formation, limiting the hypothesized beneficial effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare and deposit two sets of HEA coatings: (i) baseline composition (no dopant) and (ii) systematically increasing dopant content (e.g., 2 at.% increments up to 10 at.%). Perform identical tribological tests on both sets under controlled loads and contact conditions.
measurements: Coefficient of friction evolution via pin-on-disk or ball-on-disk testing
Wear volume (or wear rate) measured by profilometry
Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) and composition mapping (EDS) of the worn surfaces and cross sections to evaluate tribofilm presence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If doped coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate or enhanced tribofilm stability relative to the baseline under these testing conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. However, coatings of high-performance HEAs on low-cost substrates can be considered as an economically viable way forward to counter the drawbacks of the coatings employed in harsh environments, such as commercial coatings for cutting tools, extrusion dies,

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

occupying_moves.lever: Varying the fraction of a key element in the high-entropy-alloy coating (composition)
occupying_moves.technique: Deposition of coatings with controlled dopant levels, followed by systematic wear testing (e.g., pin-on-disk) and microstructural analyses (SEM/EDS/TEM)
occupying_moves.conditions: Room-temperature sliding tests at industry-relevant loads and speeds, comparing coatings with incrementally varied dopant content

chosen.lever: Adjusting the alloy’s dopant content to control lattice distortion
chosen.technique: Sputter depositing high-entropy coatings with incremental doping levels, then evaluating wear performance via tribometry and post-test microstructural characterization
chosen.conditions: Representative contact pressures and sliding speeds under ambient or controlled atmosphere conditions; dopant content varied up to 10 at.%
chosen.why: This contribution most directly addresses the open question of how to isolate and test a single mechanistic hypothesis for wear performance in high-entropy-alloy coatings: that lattice distortion and the formation of stable tribofilms collectively govern wear resistance. By altering the content of a constituent element known to increase lattice distortion, the correlation between distortion-driven tribofilm stability and wear rate can be empirically assessed. If coatings with higher distortion form more durable tribofilms and exhibit lower wear, it supports the hypothesis over the tested composition range (up to ~10 at.% doping). Contrarily, if enhanced distortion fails to reduce wear or stabilize tribo-layers, the hypothesis is refuted.
